hook: A century before electronic computers existed, Lovelace saw what they would become. Her 1843 notes on Babbage's Analytical Engine contain the first published algorithm written for a machine, and, more radically, the first argument that such machines could work on any symbol, not just numbers. Every general-purpose computer vindicates that insight.
name: Ada Lovelace

quote.text: The Analytical Engine has no pretensions whatever to originate anything. It can do whatever we know how to order it to perform.
quote.context: Note G, from her notes on the Analytical Engine, 1843

reading.body:
Ada Lovelace's 1843 notes established two ideas that define every computing system built since: that a machine can operate on any symbol under rules, not only on numbers, and that such a machine cannot originate anything beyond what it is instructed to do.

Both ideas came from a single document, her annotated translation of Luigi Menabrea's description of Babbage's Analytical Engine. The translation itself was an act of original work, expanding the source text threefold through notes A to G. Note G contained a step-by-step method for computing Bernoulli numbers, the first published algorithm written for a machine. The broader claim, that the Engine could manipulate symbols the way a Jacquard loom manipulates threads, prefigured symbolic computation by a century. That framing sits at the root of everything from programming languages to the reasoning systems now running on modern AI hardware.

Her caution is equally durable. The statement that the Engine can do only what it is ordered to perform became the direct target of Turing's 1950 argument, and the data notes it remains contested in AI research today. The data does not connect Lovelace to compute infrastructure, power, or the physical constraints on scaling, nor should it: her contribution was entirely conceptual, made before electrical machines existed. What the data does establish is that the conceptual foundation for general-purpose computation, including the debate over whether machines can think, was laid by one person working with a machine that was never completed, in a single year.

timeline.event: Meets Charles Babbage at seventeen and sees the Difference Engine
timeline.impact: Begins the collaboration that defines her work

timeline.event: Resumes advanced study under Augustus De Morgan
timeline.impact: Builds the mathematical footing for the notes

timeline.event: Publishes the annotated translation with Notes A-G
timeline.impact: First published algorithm; theory of general-purpose computation
Work lies dormant until the computing age rediscovers it

timeline.event: U.S. Department of Defense names the Ada language for her
timeline.impact: Formal recognition as programming's founding figure

quick_facts: Wrote the first published algorithm intended for a machine, the notes to Babbage's Analytical Engine (1843)
First to argue a computing machine could manipulate symbols beyond numbers, music included
Daughter of the poet Lord Byron; tutored by mathematician Augustus De Morgan
The Ada programming language (U.S. DoD, 1980) is named for her

achievements.title: Notes on the Analytical Engine (1843)
achievements.impact: Her translation of Menabrea's paper tripled in length with her own notes A through G, turning an engineering description into a theory of general computation.

achievements.title: Note G: the first published machine algorithm
achievements.impact: A step-by-step method for computing Bernoulli numbers on the Engine, recognized as the first published program.

achievements.title: The 'poetical science' thesis
achievements.impact: Her claim that the Engine could act on symbols under rules, weaving 'algebraical patterns' the way the Jacquard loom weaves flowers, prefigured symbolic computation and, by extension, AI.

achievements.title: The Lovelace objection
achievements.impact: Her caution that the Engine 'can do whatever we know how to order it to perform' framed the machine-originality debate Turing answered directly in 1950, and that AI researchers still argue.
